allow: Shell(cd /Users/mazzamabduljabbar/Documents/Repositories/personal/go-bootkit && gh issue create --title "workerpool: async work distribution module for bulk job processing" --label ready-for-agent --body "$(cat <<'EOF' ## Problem Statement The framework is purely request-response. `ApplicationRunner` manages long-lived infrastructure components (`HTTPServer`, `PostgresDB`, `RedisCache`), but there is no seam for async work distribution. A B2B client submitting 1k–100k QR codes for packaging must complete the entire batch within the HTTP server's timeout window, or the request dies. Every bulk job needs its own goroutine-pool, backpressure channel, drain-on-stop logic, and health checks — repeated in every service. ## Solution A `WorkerPool` module that plugs into the existing `core.Component` seam of `ApplicationRunner`. It accepts jobs via `Submit`, processes them with N goroutine workers through a `Processor` implementation, and exposes progress via `Status`. The Queue — how jobs are stored and delivered — sits behind an adapter seam with an in-memory channel adapter now, and a Redis streams adapter to follow. The framework owns concurrency, backpressure, drain-on-stop, panic recovery, health checks, and lifecycle. The application owns what a job *is* and what *doing* one means. ## User Stories 1. As a service developer, I want to submit a job by passing a payload and receiving a job ID, so that I can hand off bulk work without blocking the request goroutine. 2. As a service developer, I want `Submit` to return an error when the queue is at capacity, so that I can respond 503 instead of silently queueing unboundedly. 3. As a service developer, I want to query the status of a job by its ID, so that I can report progress to my client (Pending / Running / Completed / Failed). 4. As a service developer, I want to define what a job does by implementing a one-method `Processor` interface, so that the framework never needs to know my domain. 5. As a service developer, I want the pool to process jobs concurrently across N workers, so that bulk batches complete in parallel rather than serially. 6. As a service developer, I want to configure the worker count via an option, so that I can tune throughput against my infrastructure. 7. As a service developer, I want jobs that panic in the processor to be recovered, marked Failed, and logged, so that one bad job cannot kill a worker. 8. As a service developer, I want jobs that return an error from the processor to be Nacked and marked Failed, so that I can observe and retry them later. 9. As a service developer, I want the pool to drain in-flight jobs on shutdown and then stop, so that SIGTERM does not lose work mid-processing. 10. As a service developer, I want the pool to register liveness and readiness checks via `healthkit.StandardChecks`, so that it behaves like every other infrastructure component. 11. As a service developer, I want the pool to embed `core.Lifecycle`, so that start/stop/ready semantics are identical to `HTTPServer`, `PostgresDB`, and `RedisCache`. 12. As a service developer, I want structured per-job logging (job ID, worker ID, outcome), so that I can trace a batch from submission to completion. 13. As a service developer, I want the in-memory Queue adapter to be usable from my tests, so that I can verify my `Processor` end-to-end without Redis. 14. As a service developer, I want `Submit` and `Status` to accept a `context.Context`, so that cancellation and deadlines propagate naturally. 15. As an operator, I want the pool to report its readiness honestly, so that orchestrators do not route load to a pool whose workers have all exited. 16. As an operator, I want the pool's worker count and queue capacity to be configurable at construction, so that I can right-size per environment without code changes. 17. As a service developer, I want a panic in one job to be isolated to that job, so that the worker loop continues processing subsequent jobs. 18. As a service developer, I want the module to live in the workspace like `cachekit`/`databasekit`/`serverkit`, so that it has its own module boundary, version, and tests. ## Implementation Decisions ### New `workerpool` workspace module A new Go module in the repository workspace, following the existing per-package module convention (`go.mod` per kit, wired via `go.work`). Depends on `core` for `Lifecycle`, the `Component` contract, and `healthkit.StandardChecks`. No other kit dependencies. ### WorkerPool is a deep module at the `core.Component` seam - Embeds `core.Lifecycle` for start/stop/ready — start spawns the worker goroutines, stop cancels the worker context and waits for in-flight jobs to drain. - Implements the `Component` contract (`Name`, `HealthChecks`) so `ApplicationRunner` manages it like any other component. - Health checks delegate to `healthkit.StandardChecks` (liveness no-op, readiness timed check). - Constructor accepts a `Queue` and a `Processor`; both are dependencies, never created internally (matches the codebase-wide "accept dependencies, don't create them" pattern). ### Public interface — deliberately small - `Submit(ctx, payload []byte) (jobID string, err error)` — the only write path. Creates the job, enqueues it, returns the ID. Errors when the queue is at capacity or the context is cancelled (backpressure surfaces to the caller as an error). - `Status(ctx, jobID string) (JobStatus, error)` — the only read path. Returns Pending / Running / Completed / Failed (or Unknown for a job the queue does not know). - Options: `WithWorkers(n)` and `WithLogger(*slog.Logger)`. Default worker count is 1. Default logger discards. ### `Queue` interface — the adapter seam Five methods: `Enqueue(ctx, Job) error`, `Dequeue(ctx) (Job, error)`, `Ack(ctx, jobID) error`, `Nack(ctx, jobID) error`, `Status(ctx, jobID) (JobStatus, error)`. Semantics: - `Enqueue` blocks until capacity is available or the context is cancelled. - `Dequeue` blocks until a job is available or the context is cancelled (cancellation signals worker shutdown). - `Ack` marks a job Completed; `Nack` marks it Failed. - `Job` carries an ID (UUID), the payload bytes, and a created timestamp. No domain knowledge. Two adapters justify the seam: the in-memory adapter (dev/tests, this spec) and the Redis streams adapter (prod, separate follow-up). One adapter is hypothetical; we deliberately ship the seam with one adapter only after the second is planned. ### `Processor` interface — one method, application-owned `Process(ctx context.Context, payload []byte) error`. Defined in the framework, implemented in the application. One adapter (the QR generator) means the implementation does not belong in the framework. Returning an error → Nack; panicking → recovered, Nack, logged. ### Worker loop - N goroutines each loop on `Dequeue` → `Process` → `Ack`/`Nack`. - Per-job panic recovery via `defer recover()` — the panic is logged with the job ID and worker ID, the job is Nacked, and the worker loop continues. - On `Stop`: the worker context is cancelled, `Dequeue` returns the context error, each worker returns, and the pool waits on a WaitGroup before stopping. - At-least-once delivery semantics: a Nacked job may be re-observed by the adapter. Idempotency is the Processor's responsibility (documented, not enforced). ### Backpressure Capacity lives in the Queue adapter, not the pool. The in-memory adapter is a buffered channel of configurable capacity. When full, `Enqueue` blocks, so `Submit` blocks; the HTTP handler surfaces this as 503. This keeps the pool simple — one backpressure mechanism, defined by the adapter. ## Testing Decisions ### Single seam: the WorkerPool interface All behavior is tested through `Submit` / `Status` and the `core.Component` lifecycle, with the in-memory adapter and a fake Processor supplied as dependencies. The interface is the test surface; worker internals are never reached into. What makes a good test: exercises only external behavior — job lifecycle transitions (Pending → Running → Completed/Failed), drain-on-stop, panic isolation, backpressure at capacity, worker-count parallelism. No tests reach into unexported fields. ### What gets tested - **workerpool package**: lifecycle behavior via the single seam — submit/status round-trip, concurrency (N workers process M jobs), panic recovery without worker death, error → Failed, drain-on-stop waits for in-flight jobs, backpressure when the queue is full, context cancellation on submit. Prior art: `core/runner_test.go` (lifecycle/error propagation) and `core/lifecycle_test.go` (exactly-once stop, context forwarding). - **adapter/memory package**: package-level tests for the adapter itself — enqueue/dequeue blocking, status transitions, capacity-full behavior. Small and self-contained. - **Integration with `ApplicationRunner`**: register the pool as a `core.Component` alongside a fake service, verify start order, shutdown ordering, and health-check registration. Prior art: `core/runner_test.go` health-check propagation tests. ### Test style Standard `testing` with `testify/assert`, matching the codebase convention. Fake Processor is a tiny function type implementing `Process`. No integration tests requiring Redis — the in-memory adapter keeps the suite hermetic. ## Out of Scope - Redis streams Queue adapter (planned follow-up — build when the second adapter is actually needed for multi-instance production). - Retry with exponential backoff, dead-letter queues, and job priorities. - Metrics instrumentation (separate observability candidate from the architecture review). - Job scheduling / cron / periodic work. - Tenant-scoped rate limiting (separate candidate). - Multi-instance coordination (consumer-group semantics belong to the Redis adapter). ## Further Notes Originated from the architecture review for a B2B QR-generation platform (1k–100k codes per client). The WorkerPool is the top-recommended deepening: it converts the framework from request-response scaffolding into a work-distribution platform, and the other candidates (batch cache ops, rate limiting, metrics) amplify it. Naming follows the existing kit convention. The `Queue` seam follows the two-adapter rule: the memory adapter ships now because the Redis adapter is planned, not hypothetical. EOF )")
